content.text:
# A History of tmux

## Before the multiplexer

To understand tmux, start with the problem it solves. Early Unix systems gave a user one terminal session per login, and that was often a physical terminal or a serial line. A user who wanted several shells had to open several connections, and a dropped connection lost everything running in it. A long compile, a text editor session, or a process that had taken hours to set up died with the line.

Terminal multiplexers answered this by putting a program between the user's terminal and the shells. The multiplexer owns the pseudo-terminals, so the shells keep running when the user disconnects, and it can show several of them through one real terminal. The idea is older than most current users of the tool. The best-known early multiplexer is GNU Screen, written by Oliver Laumann in 1987 and later maintained by the GNU project under Juergen Weigert and others. Screen became the standard answer for decades. It was widely installed, worked over slow links, and let people detach from a session on one machine and reattach from another.

Screen's weaknesses were real, though. Its codebase was large and old, and its terminal emulation had many edge cases that were hard to fix without breaking something else. Its configuration language was idiosyncratic, its handling of window titles and character sets was tangled, and its design had accumulated decades of compatibility layers. Many developers used it daily and still found it frustrating. The question of what a modern multiplexer should look like was open, and the answer came from a developer who had spent a lot of time with screen.

## Nicholas Marriott and the first commit

tmux was written by Nicholas Marriott, a developer working in the OpenBSD ecosystem. Marriott began the project in 2007. The name stands for "terminal multiplexer." Its goals were to be a clean replacement for Screen, with a simpler codebase, a more careful model of terminal behavior, and a configuration system that would be easier to understand.

Marriott released tmux under the ISC license, a permissive license similar to the BSD licenses. That choice made tmux easy to package and embed. It also fit the OpenBSD culture of code that is small, careful, and readable. The early releases were modest. The first versions had a single window per session with multiple panes, a command prompt, and a basic key-binding system. What set the design apart was its architecture, which mattered more than any single feature.

## The client-server design

tmux is split into a server and clients. When the user first runs tmux, it starts a server process in the background. That server owns every session, window, and pane, and it owns the pseudo-terminals the shells run in. A client process attaches to the server over a Unix domain socket, usually in a directory under `/tmp`, and forwards keystrokes to it. The server redraws the screen and sends the result back to the client.

This design is one of the main reasons tmux feels different from Screen. A client can detach without affecting the server, and the server keeps running after every client is gone. Several clients can attach to the same session at once, which is useful for pair programming, monitoring, and remote support. The same session can look different on two screens of different sizes, and the server keeps its own model of each window.

The split also made the code easier to reason about. The server keeps a structured model of sessions, windows, and panes. The client handles only terminal input and output. Terminal emulation sits in the server, where it can be tested without a real terminal attached. Marriott rebuilt the terminal layer around an explicit model of the emulated screen, which made many behaviors predictable in a way the older code was not.

## The early years and OpenBSD

tmux grew up in the OpenBSD community, and that shaped its character. OpenBSD's developers are known for conservative code, secure defaults, and a strong preference for removing unnecessary complexity. Those values matched Marriott's goals. Early tmux releases were distributed through OpenBSD ports, and the project's mailing lists and bug trackers were tied to that community.

The early codebase relied on the libevent library for event handling, which kept the server's input and output loops manageable. The project also had to handle the many variations in terminal capabilities that existed in the late 2000s. Terminfo entries differed between systems, and tmux had to present a consistent interface whether the user was on Linux, OpenBSD, macOS, or a remote host.

Adoption grew slowly and then accelerated. Developers who had used Screen for years tried tmux because it was simpler to configure and felt faster. Package maintainers in Linux distributions added it to their repositories. Over time tmux became the default multiplexer on many systems, and the question of which tool to install shifted from "screen or tmux" to "tmux, unless you have a reason not to."

## The 1.x series

The 1.x releases were when tmux stopped being an experiment and became a tool many people depended on. Development focused on stability, terminal compatibility, and the core features users expected from a multiplexer: named sessions, multiple windows with independent layouts, copy mode for scrolling and selecting text, and a command language that could be scripted.

Copy mode is worth singling out. Screen had a scrollback and a copy mechanism, but tmux's copy mode fit naturally with vi-style and Emacs-style keybindings, and it became a common reason to choose tmux. Users could scroll through output, search with familiar keys, and copy text into a paste buffer that the server kept. The paste buffer was shared across sessions, which made copying between shells easy.

The configuration system also matured. A user's `~/.tmux.conf` file could set options, bind keys, and run commands at startup. The syntax was simple enough to learn in a few minutes and powerful enough to build elaborate setups. Many users shared their configuration files, and the habit of publishing dotfiles, which was growing across Unix culture at the time, made tmux configuration one of the most visible parts of the community.

## The 2.x series and mouse support

tmux 2.0 was released in 2015. Its most visible change for many users was the move toward modern terminal behavior and a cleaner default setup, but the release also reflected a more mature project. The codebase had been refactored, and the command set was more consistent. Maintainers were paying more attention to documentation, release discipline, and compatibility across platforms.
